question: Is it permissible to stop people from coming for Hajj because of the COVID pandemic?
answer:
Regarding whether it is permissible or not: at the end of the day, we have to deal with what we are given. I'm not in charge of this decision. It is the Ministry of Hajj and the Ministry of Health that has decided this. And I am sympathetic to it overall. I understand that it is not the wisest at this stage to have millions of people from across the globe come together.

The question of whether this has ever occurred in the past or not: well, it is true that in Islamic history there have been a number of times where the Hajj has been severely impeded. For example, in the year 317 Hijrah, there was an internal revolt, a fanatical sect called the Qaramita, or the Carmathians. They were a very extreme fringe sect that were on the esoteric branches of Islam, and they had very bizarre beliefs, such that they were not considered mainstream Muslims. And they attacked the Ka'bah during Hajj in the year 317. Very tragic state of affairs. They actually, believe it or not, destroyed sections of the Ka'bah. They hijacked the Black Stone, the Hajar al-Aswad, and they took it to their place in the region of Bahrain, and they built a false Ka'bah over there. And so for around 20 years, there was no Black Stone.

In fact, in that Hajj in 317, very tragic story, they actually massacred the pilgrims in front of the Ka'bah, and they, a'udhu billah, a'udhu billah, they stuffed the well of Zamzam with their dead bodies. These are stories that a lot of times nobody's even heard of, but these are well-known incidents in our Islamic history, and they wreaked havoc and terror for a number of years. And so after that year, when the people heard about this, they were terrified to even go. So for a number of years, the Hajj dwindled to a very small quantity.

As well, multiple times there were a number of civil wars that took place in the Muslim world that prevented large caravans from coming. In the third and the fourth centuries, multiple times, specific regions in the Muslim world were not able to send their hujjaj. Obviously in the Mongol invasion as well, when the Mongols invaded, Genghis Khan, when he invaded, the entire Muslim world was disrupted, and for a number of years the Hajj was very much symbolic; very small groups of people came.

Also in 1798, when Napoleon invaded Egypt, there were no hujjaj that went from the entire North African region. So imagine, from Morocco all the way, because the hujjaj would go through Egypt when they come to the Hijaz, to Mecca and Medina. And so when Napoleon invaded, one of the major arteries of Hajj was completely disrupted. Now, Hajj went on, but it was not anywhere near the numbers that they were accustomed to.

As well, throughout Islamic history there have been a number of pandemics, or rather I should say cholera outbreaks, because that's usually what occurred: there were a number of deadly bouts of cholera, and these affected the hujjaj. The famous Egyptian historian al-Jabarti, he mentions that in the year 1831 CE, basically 150 years ago, 170 years ago, three fourths of the hujjaj died in Hajj because of an outbreak of cholera. And in 1865, it killed almost 20,000 people at Hajj, and in those days Hajj was around 80,000, so like one fourth of the hujjaj. So basically within 30 years, three fourths and then one fourth of the hujjaj were wiped out. And by the way, in 1865, the Hajj actually caused, meaning the people that were interacting in Hajj, when they returned back, it caused this cholera outbreak to spread across the globe, so much so that they even said that eventually that outbreak even reached the Western world and America.

And of course, at this point in time, the British and the French are ruling large segments of the Muslim world, so they're taking charge of the Hajj in the 18th, 19th century. And it's interesting that in the 19th century, meaning the 1800s, after the mutiny, after the British Raj in 1856, 1857, when the British took over, the British had to organize the pilgrims of India, which was the largest group, or one of the largest groups, of pilgrims. And because the British are in charge, they have to have a ministry of Hajj, believe it or not. They actually had a person stationed in Jeddah, a British person, non-Muslim, that's in charge of the hujjaj and monitoring them.

And because cholera was one of the biggest problems, there were attempts to curb the quantity of hujjaj. And of course this caused a huge backlash, because the Muslims felt, who are you to tell us whether we can go or not? And the British felt that we are in charge of you, and you're affecting our ships because you're coming on our ships; your cholera is going to affect all of us. And so there were always tensions here and there. This isn't the first time this tension is taking place.

And an interesting incident took place in 1899 that the famous Rashid Rida, the great 'alim of the last century, discusses: in 1899, because of the spread of cholera, French authorities attempted to curtail the Hajj. They don't have the right to ban, but they're ruling over countries. They're ruling over North Africa; they have sections of Egypt and whatnot. And so they attempted to curb the Hajj from their own parties. They can't stop it in Mecca and Medina, but they can stop it in their own lands, or the colonized lands, I should say, that are ruled by these colonial powers. And the French attempted to ban their peoples from going for Hajj.

And this caused a huge outbreak, because again, the French were invaders, the French were colonizers, and the Muslim 'ulama felt, who are you to tell us that we cannot go for Hajj? And this issue reached the Grand Mufti of Egypt, and great 'ulama gathered together in 1899, and they discussed whether the French ban should be effective or not. And Shaykh Rashid Rida talks about this in one of his writings in Majallat al-Manar. He mentions that the Ra'is Majlis al-Nuzzar and the Qadi and the Shaykh al-Azhar and the Mufti ad-Diyar al-Misriyya, they came together. Amongst them, he said, was Shaykh Abdurrahman al-Nawawi and Shaykh Abdul Qadir al-Rafi'i and others of that era. And they all agreed that the authorities in France had no right to tell the Muslims whether they should or should not go for Hajj. And they said that just because there's a cholera outbreak in the Hijaz, this should not stop the Muslims from going for Hajj, and whoever wants to go for Hajj, even if there is a sickness, then they should be allowed to go.

Now, having said this, it should also be mentioned that Shaykh Rashid and others mentioned that the French had a sinister motive. It wasn't the health of the hujjaj. In 1899, there was a lot of anti-British and anti-French sentiment going on, and there were people that wanted to get rid of these colonial powers, but they weren't allowed to meet in France, or, I should say, in the French-occupied territories. And so Mecca became a safe haven for political dissidents across the globe to come together and to hatch plans to basically be anti-British and anti-French. And so the notion was, they're not stopping the Muslims from going for Hajj; they're stopping political dissidents from meeting up. And so that was the goal there.

In any case, all of this is down history lane. And by the way, just FYI, 100 years ago, as you should all know, this is something by now everybody should know, the closest pandemic that we should be familiar with is that which took place in 1917 and 1918, the Spanish influenza, which was global, and it was from the same strain as the COVID-19; the same strain of virus that is there in the Spanish influenza is now present as well in the COVID. And in 1917 and 1918, when the Sharifs of Mecca ruled over that region, they did not prevent the hujjaj from coming, even though the numbers were less than usual.

Now, all of this is history. At the end of the day, I'm not in charge. It wasn't my decision. Whether I agree or not doesn't change the fact that Hajj has temporarily been suspended for people outside the country. As for those inside the country, there will be a very small amount (one report said 1,000, one report said 10,000 people), just a symbolic amount, that the Hajj will take place. It does appear to me, and Allah knows best, that this might be the first time in all of Islamic history that the Hajj has been curtailed in this manner.

But do realize as well that the reason why it is even possible for this to happen is because of the nation states and the visas and the transportation. I mean, you couldn't have stopped the Hajj 500 years ago even if you wanted to. Hujjaj would come from Morocco; they wouldn't know what's going on. It's going to take three months for them to get to Mecca. Visas and stamping them: all of this is now modern stuff. Getting on the airplane, making sure you have your paperwork: you couldn't have done this even 200 years ago.

So this notion of, is there precedent or not: as I have mentioned in my previous lectures about this COVID crisis, it is not my philosophy that we need precedent in the first place. To be brutally honest, I am not of the mindset that we need a precedent for every single fatwa that is given. As I said in a previous lecture, this COVID crisis really has demarcated two paradigms within the scholarly community. There is one paradigm that is completely averse to any change whatsoever, and they're always looking to the past and always looking for precedent, and they're saying, who before us allowed this? And I understand and I respect that very philosophically conservative frame of mind.

But the flip side is: why are we bound by the views of people 500 years ago, 1,000 years ago, with our utmost respect to them? Our knowledge and our circumstances have changed. And had they been alive right now, it is my belief that they would have taken advantage of the knowledge that we have. So I don't need precedent in this regard. Rather, the scholars of our times — we should not do it single-handedly; neither I nor any scholar should just break away from the chains of all scholarship. We should always have groups of 'ulama, groups of people, come together and discuss these modern issues.

And by and large, as you're aware, the majority of the scholars of our times have agreed to this ban on foreigners coming, because we don't want to exacerbate the situation. We now know how these viruses are spread. We know much more about the transmission and safety mechanisms, and this was not known even a hundred years ago. Even in the Spanish influenza, when it occurred, we didn't know what we know now. And so we want to be safe here. And of the primary pillars of our Shari'ah is the preservation of life.

And as for the Hajj, it is not being stopped. There will be a group of people that are going to be going. The Hajj will take place, whether it's 1,000, whether it's 10,000. Alhamdulillah, the adhan will be called; people will be in Arafat.

And here's the beauty. Our Prophet ﷺ said, as we're all familiar with, "Innamal a'malu bin-niyyat, wa innama li-kullimri'in ma nawa": all actions will be judged by intentions, and everyone will get what they intended. And so, I was intending to go for Hajj. I had a group of 200 people that were going to go with me for Hajj. So many people were intending to go for Hajj. Inshallah, be certain that you had the intention; Allah will reward you for that intention.

There's a hadith by Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As: our Prophet ﷺ said that if the Muslim is sick, Allah 'azza wa jall will say, "Write for him all that he used to do in the best of manners. Go ahead and write it for him." Meaning, the point of the hadith is: suppose you used to pray extra prayers, then you fell sick with a fever and you weren't able to pray those nafl prayers. Allah will say to the angels, go ahead and write those nafl prayers and give him the maximum reward, just because he had that intention to do it, but something came in the way. So here as well we have the intention to go for Hajj, and circumstances came between us and the Hajj.

So, Allah decrees, and whatever He wills happens. We accept the decree of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, and we understand that this was a decision that does make logistical sense. There's no need to prolong this crisis as it is. It has created world havoc. Why should we make it worse? Because you have 3 million people that are going to come, and these are all going to go back to their lands. It is a recipe for disaster.

Anybody who has gone for Hajj — and I've been, alhamdulillah, to more than 15 Hajj, may Allah accept them, or even one of them — but anybody who goes for Hajj knows you are congested. You're living in tight, cramped quarters. You're going to be in crowds that you've never seen in your life. You're in a tent with 15, 20 people; the restroom facilities... I mean, you are asking for disaster with that congestion. It does not make any sense. This is a global pandemic. Why do you want to prolong and delay the lifting of it?

So I understand; obviously we're all saddened. I was looking forward to Hajj. I needed a break from all that is going on. I needed to go and make du'a to Allah and stand in Arafat. I was looking forward to it. Allah knows I was looking forward to it. Qaddar Allahu wa ma sha'a fa'al: Allah 'azza wa jall has decreed. So inshallah ta'ala, I'm going to go, inshallah, next year. And all of you who wanted to go this year, you got the reward, and then try to go next year.
